findings.title: KeyError crash when integration metadata lacks 'sender'
findings.body: GitHubInstallation.dispatch accesses `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` unconditionally when an active Integration exists. `sender` is only added to metadata when the installation webhook (or build_integration) recorded it; an Integration created through other paths (older records predating this field, or where the webhook payload had no sender) will not have the key. The result is an unhandled KeyError/TypeError that surfaces as a 500 error instead of the intended error page. Use `integration.metadata.get("sender", {}).get("login")` and decide how to treat a missing sender.

findings.title: Sender-verification is skipped when the Integration row does not yet exist
findings.body: The authenticated-user check only runs in the branch where an Integration with a matching external_id already exists. On a brand-new GitHub App installation, the Integration row is created asynchronously by the installation webhook; if the webhook has not been processed yet when the user (or an attacker who knows the installation_id) completes the pipeline, `Integration.DoesNotExist` is raised and `pipeline.next_step()` is returned with no sender comparison at all. This is a race that bypasses exactly the mismatch check this PR is meant to add: an attacker who learns a victim's installation_id and reaches the pipeline before the webhook lands can link the integration without ever being verified as the installer.

findings.title: get_user_info and token-exchange network failures are unhandled
findings.body: In OAuthLoginView.dispatch, `safe_urlopen` (line 423) and `get_user_info(payload["access_token"])` (line 434) can raise on network/API errors (timeouts, 5xx from GitHub). Only the body-parsing is wrapped in try/except. An exception here propagates and yields a 500 to the user instead of the friendly 'Invalid installation request' error page shown for the other failure modes described in the PR. Wrap the token exchange and user-info call so failures return the same error response.

findings.title: State parameter compared with non-constant-time equality
findings.body: `request.GET.get("state") != pipeline.signature` uses ordinary string comparison. The pipeline signature is a secret-derived CSRF token; using `hmac.compare_digest` (as done in other OAuth flows in the codebase) avoids leaking signature bytes via timing. Low practical risk over the network, but it is the standard hardening for this exact check.
